label: 00 · INTRO
text: Meet the Disroop Sensor Playground. A place where motion becomes a controller.

label: 01 · THE PLAYGROUND
text: The premise is simple. You hold a sensor in your hand. You move. And a game in the browser answers. Two games, one handheld device, and the full engineering trail behind it, all on a single page.

label: 02 · THE CUBE
text: It began with a cube. The Nordic Thingy fifty-two streams acceleration, gyro, compass, temperature and pressure over Bluetooth Low Energy, live into a web dashboard and an Android app. Factory firmware. Nothing to flash.

label: 03 · EXPERIMENT: TENNIS
text: Experiment one: tennis. The cube becomes the racket. You swing, the motion sensor detects the hit, and the ball flies across a floodlit court.

label: 04 · EXPERIMENT: SKI
text: Experiment two: the Lauberhorn downhill. Tilt to steer. Nose down to tuck. A sharp jolt to jump. Your wrist is the skier.

label: 05 · DEVICE: MOTION ONE
text: Then the cube was not enough. Enter Motion One, a handheld controller designed from scratch. Button cap, top shell, circuit board, battery, and a bottom shell with clips. It speaks the same Bluetooth profile as the Thingy, so the games run unchanged.

label: 06 · ENGINEERING TRAIL
text: The documentation is unusually honest. Every claim carries a label: source, calculation, or assumption. Circuit board revision three, with a bill of materials checked against live supplier stock, calculated at about twenty dollars in parts per device. And a housing printed in nylon powder, by selective laser sintering.

label: 07 · OUTLOOK
text: And the remarkable part: AI agents built all of it, with every tool running in Docker. A playground, yes. But also a preview of how AI crosses from the screen into the physical world.
